cards.note: Found in Western Visayas, these trikes feature a passenger compartment that resembles a spaceship, with a distinctly aerodynamic design.
Bataan has these double vertical-windowed trikes, and they’re very concentrated within Bataan

The standard Bicol high-roof trike features many large, squarish windows for both driver and passenger, a large connecting window between them, and additional windows on the sides and rear. The passenger side is open and spacious.
The standard Bicol mid-roof trike shares many characteristics with the high-roof version: numerous large windows, a connecting window between driver and passenger, and a spacious passenger area.
Bohol trikes are large and boxy, with one large window and a crown. Their defining feature is an additional window located below the driver’s position.
This tuk-tuk–style trike is exclusive to Bohol. It features small horn-like mirrors at the front and small side windows. From the back, it looks fairly generic but includes two rear windows.

Bukidnon trikes are long and distinctive, featuring a large square main window with two side windows next to it, forming a trifold layout. They often lean backward, usually have a crown on top, and may include side windows at the rear. These trikes are found in northern Mindanao and on Camiguin Island.

This is the standard Calabarzon trike. Key features include the padded coverings above both the passenger and driver, the curved bar in front of the driver, and the shape of the passenger car with a belt running beneath the window. There are a few minor variations in shape (such as a window above the driver, below the passenger, or differences in car size), but most of these are not strongly regional within Calabarzon. I noticed that the majority of these trikes have a silver, mirror-like, metallic finish.
Very common in the Davao region and also frequent in Butuan City, these trikes resemble small cars in both shape and appearance. They are easy to recognize and come in a wide range of colors.
Caraga trikes feature two distinct, squarish passenger windows, with a flat window beneath them. Several variations of this style exist.
These trikes feature square, plane-like windows and a crown on the roof. Many variations can be found within the same area.
These trikes have a striking design, with a pyramid-like passenger compartment. In some cases, the window is divided into two sections.
On Cebu Island, some trikes feature a roof made from fabric or tissue-like material, resembling an umbrella. This style is extremely common across the island and can be found almost everywhere.

Cotabato trikes sometimes have a number plate mounted on the roof. They feature one or two windows that slope slightly forward, while the body beneath the windows slopes backward. The flat roof also leans backward.

These high-roof trikes feature crowns above both the driver and passenger windows. If you see a high-roof trike with crowns, you are likely in the northern part of the country. The crown design is very distinctive, even across different body shapes.

This is the typical Davao City trike. It features two large windows, a bar beneath the windows, a large flat roof, and windows that slope backward. Some versions include a crown or a protruding element at the bottom (more common in downtown Davao), but the overall shape is the defining characteristic.

Along the Davao Oriental coast, trikes with flat roofs and windows divided into two sections are common. A large number plate is mounted beneath the windows, and the trikes are often brightly colored.
Similar to the leather-back trike, but with the difference that the leather also covers the roof. It can be found near Laoag City.

This trike is unique to General Santos. The main window extends outward at an angle, the roof slopes forward, and the window often includes two or three horizontal lines. Beneath the main window are two small auxiliary windows. A specific shade of blue is common in downtown General Santos, while an orange variant is exclusive to Polomolok, just north of the city.
On Guimaras Island, trikes tend to have rounded or aerodynamic shapes.
The passenger side features a hexagonal-shaped window at the rear. This type of trike is common in the northern part of the country.
These trikes feature a long, box-shaped low roof. A crown may appear on the passenger side, and a number plate is often visible beneath a small passenger window. They appear in various colors.

Trikes near Lake Lanao feature a very specific vertical passenger window and vertical bars on the passenger side. The driver’s window is more horizontal or square-shaped, and the roof is black on both sides.

The leather-back trike can be found in the northern part of the country as well as in central Luzon, particularly in the Ilocos region. The back of the trike is easily recognizable by its black leather.

Trikes are far more common in Leyte than in Mindanao, where they tend to cluster around main roads. In Leyte, they are ubiquitous—even in rural areas. The standard Leyte trike features two slightly outward-tilting windows, a large curved crown on top, and a roof that slopes backward. The body shape beneath the windows is the easiest way to identify them

This is the main Masbate trike design. The driver’s side is fully open with a roof, while the passenger side features a large window, a crown, metal bars, and a hexagonal shape. In Masbate City, these trikes are often yellow, though other colors exist across the region.
All Mindoro trikes share a metallic design with vivid colors. Decorative metal bars are an integral part of their overall aesthetic.
Common in northern Mindanao, these trikes feature airplane-style passenger windows. There are many variations, and they appear in a wide range of colors.
These trikes feature a curved crown on top, two windows, and a large number displayed below the passenger window. They appear in many different colors.
In southern Negros, mid-roof trikes share the same retro, 1970s-inspired passenger compartment design. Some versions include an additional window on the roof.
These trikes are highly distinctive, with a passenger compartment shaped somewhat like a Japanese train car. They appear in various colors and are easy to spot across Cebu Island.
Another Cebu variant features a small horizontal window in the passenger compartment.
Here’s the northern Panay trike. He’s silly & boxy, and he’s a guy, and he’s a little short don’t make fun of him.
The passenger side features a crown on the roof, and the trike is fitted with transparent plastic protection. These trikes are unique to this region
Palawan trikes are among the most unique in the country. Their car-like shape reminiscent of a Smart car makes them immediately recognizable.
If you encounter unusually shaped high-roof trikes, chances are you are in the Romblon region or on Sibuyan Island.
Samar flat-roof trikes have a unique curved body shape that makes them easily recognizable. They are slightly wider than average and usually feature a black roof.

This type of trike that’s really small in size, has two large windows and a connecting window, and the passenger trike is very low are extremely common in Western Samar. This specific shade of red with these small details are common in Catbalogan City. These can also be identified by their silly looking singular window in the back.
South Bukidnon trikes are generally green, with a single horizontal window and a flat roof. The roof is also green and often includes metallic crossbars.
In southern Negros, trikes have a very distinctive design. The passenger compartment resembles a small 1970s-era car, often paired with a large square flat roof.
Southern Panay trikes feature a unique bumpy, curved body shape. The passenger window is a rounded square, and the driver’s side has no window.

These trikes feature a large flat black roof, a small side window, and no lines on the main window. They are mainly found in Sultan Kudarat. Green versions with blue “POBLACION” text are specific to Isulan, while more colorful variants with numbers on the roof are unique to Tacurong City.

This downtown Surigao trike features an extremely long window with two or three horizontal lines, a small bumper beneath the window, and a rear bar with a side window. The roof slopes backward less than other styles, giving it a very distinct shape. These trikes appear in many different colors.

Trikes with an umbrella-style roof can be found in the Zamboanga Peninsula and across Mindanao. These trikes are easily recognizable by their umbrella-shaped roofs. This type is common in Pagadian City and very common in Cotabato City.

Zamboanga City has a wide variety of trikes, but this flat-roof model is distinctive. It often features a white line separating the passenger and driver sections, horizontally shaped windows, and elaborate decorations. Zamboanga trikes are especially known for their bright, colorful designs and ornamental details.

This is essentially the only high-roof trike variant found throughout the Zamboanga Peninsula. The passenger window resembles an airplane window, the roof slopes backward, and the body slightly bulges beneath the window.
